Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

table.title: Children’s understanding of comparative “more” in the numerical and temporal dimensions
table.research_questions:
One possibility is that children learn and apply the meaning of “more” to the numerical and temporal dimensions at once, consistent with a simultaneous account of acquisition. If so, we would expect similar performance in the Numerical and Temporal Quantification Tasks.

Another possibility is that children learn and apply the meaning of “more” to either the numerical or temporal dimension first, and only later to the other dimension, consistent with an incremental account of acquisition. If so, we would expect better performance on one of the quantification tasks.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
Age (2;6-4;11) X 2 (Dimension: Numerical, Temporal on Quantification Tasks). Within-subjects design with task performance as the dependent variable

See counter-balancing below
table.randomization:
The following will be randomized:

Half of the participants will receive the Numerical Quantification Task followed by the Temporal Quantification Task. The other half will receive the Temporal Quantification Task followed by the Numerical Quantification Task.

In both Quantification Tasks, the experimenter will point to (e.g., “Look, Character X is dancing, and Character Y is dancing too”)  and ask about the character on the right first (e.g., “Who did more dancing, Character X or Character Y?”) for half the participants and on the left first for the other half of participants.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.existing_data_explanation:
The data for the experiment proper have yet to be collected. However, we would like to report the results of a pilot study at this time:

We conducted a pilot study in which we showed 10 2-year-olds (mean age: 2.5 years) six videos of two experimenters performing an event, one for 4 seconds and one for 8 seconds, as in the Temporal Quantification Task. For each event, we asked the child “Who spent tiv time X?”, where X was the event (e.g., making a silly face). The child selected the experimenter who performed the event for more time 35% of the time. This suggests that in the experiment proper, if children respond accurately when asked who spent more time performing an event, their performance reflects understanding of the meaning of “more”, rather than the use of a simple heuristic of picking the person who performed the event for more time regardless of understanding the meaning of the word. This pilot study was conducted with 2-year-olds, who according to past reports do not yet understand “more”, rather than children 3 years old or older, because it is possible that acquiring the meaning of “more” leads children to respond as if tiv meant “more” (see Carey, 1978).
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be native English-speaking children between 2.5 and 5 years old. Children will be recruited from museums and preschools in the Comox Valley, Canada and San Diego, USA areas.
table.sample_size: A total of 60 children will be recruited to participate in this study.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size was determined by conducting a sensitivity power analysis using the package simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016) in which we simulated an extension of existing pilot data. Across effect sizes, we calculated power achieved for different sample sizes at a significance criterion of alpha = .05 for a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) that compared participants’ performance between the two Quantification Tasks (Numerical, Temporal). The specific GLMM structure is described in Analysis II. Via this power analysis, we determined that n = 60 is a reasonable sample size to achieve 90% power with an effect size of d = .15.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop collecting data once we reach our target sample size post exclusions.
table.manipulated_variables: Numerical or temporal dimension in the Quantification Tasks
table.measured_variables: Numerical and Temporal Quantification Tasks: Accuracy coded as 1 (correct) or 0 (incorrect)
table.statistical_tests:
1. To test how children’s comprehension of comparative “more” changes throughout the developmental period tested, we will build a base generalized linear mixed model with child’s age as a fixed factor and participant and trial as random factors:
Accuracy on Quantification Tasks ~ Child Age + (1|PID) + (1|Item)

2. To test how children’s comprehension of comparative “more” may differ between the numerical and temporal dimensions, we will add a term to the previous model:
Accuracy on Quantification Tasks ~ Child Age + Dimension (Numerical / Temporal) + (1 + Dimension | PID) + (1|Item)

3. To test how children’s comprehension may differ by dimension differently for different ages within the sample:
Accuracy on Quantification Tasks ~ Child Age * Dimension (Numerical / Temporal) + (1 + Dimension | PID) + (1|Item)

4. To test whether children make judgments of “more” greater than chance in different age groups in the sample on each task, we will conduct the following two-tailed, one-sample t-tests for the proportion of correct responses (mu = ½):
a) On the Numerical Quantification Task, for the younger half of children in the sample
b) On the Temporal Quantification Task, for the younger half of children in the sample
c) On the Numerical Quantification Task, for the older half of children in the sample
d) On the Temporal Quantification Task, for the older half of children in the sample
table.transformations: We will dummy code Dimension (reference level: Numerical).
table.inference_criteria: We will use a p = .05 alpha level.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Children who do not complete all trials of the experiment will be excluded from the analysis.
Children for whom experimenter error occurred during the experiment will be excluded from the analysis.
Children for whom parental interference occurred during the experiment will be excluded from the analysis.
table.missing_data_handling: Children who are missing data from any task will be excluded from analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses:
It is possible that there will be a quadratic relationship for the interaction between age and dimension on accuracy in the Quantification Tasks that is not captured by model number 3. If the meaning of “more” is first applied to the numerical dimension and only later to the temporal dimension, we may find that the youngest children in the sample perform similarly at chance in the two dimensions and the oldest children perform similarly near ceiling, but children in the middle of the age sample perform better on the numerical than temporal dimension. In this case, we plan on building the following model:
Accuracy on Quantification Tasks ~ poly(Child Age, 2) * Dimension (Numerical / Temporal) + (1 + Dimension | PID) + (1|Item)

table.title: Children’s understanding of comparative “more” in the numerical and temporal dimensions (Exp. 4)
table.research_questions:
If children’s “more” judgments for time in previous experiments were based upon a non-linguistic heuristic to choose the character who acted last, and not on comprehension of “more”, then we should expect children to select the person who acted last in this experiment, despite that person performing the action for less time overall.
If children’s “more” judgments for time in previous experiments were based on understanding of “more”, and not on a non-linguistic heuristic to choose the character who acted last, then children should select the person who performed the action for longer overall in this experiment.

The ability to represent temporal duration is a fundamental aspect of human cognition.

Humans encode passing time perceptually (see Grondin, 2010; Pöppel, 1997; Wittmann, 2013), but also in natural language via conventional units such as "second", "minute", and "hour" to denote precise durations, and expressions such as "more" or "longer" to compare relative durations (e.g., "John danced for more than two hours").

text.text: Although temporal language is highly frequent in early linguistic input, and time imbues every aspect of human experience, time words are mastered relatively late in acquisition (e.g., Shatz et al., 2010; Tillman & Barner, 2015; Tillman et al., 2017).

text.text: In the current study, we explored the nature of this protracted development by investigating how children learn to encode passing time with the comparative "more."

Temporal comparison provides an important test case for understanding how children encode time linguistically, because whereas lexical representations of duration like "second" and "minute" are learned relatively late in development and are not adult-like until age 6 or 7 (see Tillman & Barner, 2015), children begin to use the comparative "more" by age 3 to quantify domains like number and space (Barner & Snedeker, 2006; Gathercole, 1985; Odic et al., 2013).

text.text: Combined with the observation that humans can discriminate temporal durations non-verbally beginning in infancy (e.g., Brannon et al., 2007), this raises the possibility that children can linguistically encode and compare temporal durations relatively early in development, and before they encode absolute duration information in words like "minute" and "hour".

text.text: Given this, the current study investigated preschool-aged children's comprehension of the comparative "more" when used to evaluate relative temporal durations.
The ability to non-verbally discriminate temporal durations emerges early in development.
By 6 months of age, infants are able to discriminate durations in 2:1 ratio (e.g., 1 vs.
0.5 seconds, 3 vs.
1.5 seconds, and 4 vs. 2 seconds), dishabituating when the duration of a familiarized event changes (Brannon et al., 2007; vanMarle & Wynn, 2006).

text.text: By three years of age, children can make explicit judgments comparing the duration of two events.

For example, in a study by Droit-Volet and colleagues (2001), children as young as 3 successfully judged that a stimulus duration (e.g., a circle appearing on a screen) differed from a previously trained standard of comparison (i.e., by identifying it as not being "their" circle) when the difference between the test duration and the standard was several seconds long (e.g., 4 vs. 8 seconds).

text.text: After training, children were presented with intermediate durations (1.5-3.5 or 3-7 seconds, depending on the condition) and asked to choose which button corresponded to each.
Three-year-olds reliably classified the shorter intervals with the "short" button and longer intervals with the "long" button, demonstrating sensitivity to relative differences in duration.

While these findings demonstrate that children can discriminate perceptual durations by at least age 3, it remains unclear whether they are able to encode and compare such comparisons in a symbolic, linguistic format, and whether this differs from their ability to reason about other domains, like number or space.

Time may be especially difficult to encode linguistically because of its abstract nature: while not being a property of any individual object that we can perceive, it permeates every perceptual experience, posing a potentially difficult problem of identifying when a speaker intends to refer to time itself, rather than the objects and events that are situated within it (for discussion, see Gleitman et al., 2005; Shatz et al., 2010; Tillman & Barner, 2015; Tillman et al., 2024).

text.text: Consistent with this, previous studies find that children's learning of duration words is highly protracted.

While children produce words referring to absolute durations such as "second", "minute", and "hour" by as early as 3 years of age, they do not acquire adult-like meanings for these words until around age 7 (Grant & Suddendorf, 2011; Shatz et al., 2010; Tillman & Barner, 2015).

text.text: It is currently unknown whether children undergo a similarly protracted learning trajectory when linguistically comparing relative durations.
As in the case of learning duration words, to encode relative durations in comparative statements involving "more", children must represent the relative magnitudes of different events.

Also, they must recognize that the linguistic unit "more" can apply to durations, and that events should be measured temporally -i.e., that someone who "did more dancing", did more of the event by virtue of having spent more time doing so.
This latter process may be non-trivial, since events can be quantified by a wide range of dimensions other than time.

For example, deciding who did "more helping" or "more eating" might be judged on the basis of time, but also on, e.g., how helpful one is, or how much food they ate (see Barner et al., 2008, for evidence that adults consider multiple possible dimensions for quantifying events).

text.text: This leaves open the possibility that children do not readily select time as relevant when interpreting linguistic quantifiers like "more".

On the other hand, encoding time with "more" may be easier than learning words like "minute" or "hour", given that the latter words require learning arbitrary culturally-mediated durations that may depend on learning number words and multiplicative relations (e.g., that an hour is 60 minutes).

Whereas the comparison of relative magnitudes is commonplace in language and "more" can be applied to just about any dimension, children may not expect words to encode precise, arbitrary amounts of time.

Thus, it is possible that encoding time in comparative language emerges earlier than other forms of temporal language, and perhaps on the same timeline as comparison of other domains like number or space.

text.text: In the current study we investigated children's ability to linguistically compare relative durations in "more" constructions, and how this relates to their ability to make numerical comparisons.

In Study 1, we tested 2½ to 4-year-old children with a Temporal Quantification Task in which they judged which of two people did "more" of an action like "waving", and compared this to a Numerical Quantification Task that asked them to make quantity judgments with the comparative "more" between arrays of objects.

Because children could have succeeded on the Temporal Quantification Task in Study 1 via a bias to select the person who completed the action last, in Studies 2 and 3 we tested 3-to 4-year-old children in a Temporal Quantification Task in which the person who performed the action longer did not perform it last, removing the possibility of using such a bias.
In Study 1, we tested children's ability to make linguistic comparisons of relative durations using the word "more", and compared these temporal judgments to analogous numerical judgments.

text.text: Study 1 found two main results.
First, 3-and 4-year-olds were better than chance when making "more" judgments for temporal durations.
Second, however, 3-and 4-year-olds performed better on the Numerical Quantification Task than the Temporal Quantification Task.

Together, these results suggest that children are able to quantify temporal durations relatively early in development and may apply quantifiers such as "more" not only to more concrete domains such as number but to more abstract domains such as time as well.
There are multiple reasons why children might have performed better on numerical than temporal quantification.

One possibility is that children are able to compare relative magnitudes with "more" for number (and perhaps continuous amount; see Odic et al., 2013) first, and can only do so for time slightly later in development.
text.formatted: One possibility is that children are able to compare relative magnitudes with "more" for number (and perhaps continuous amount; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Odic et al., 2013)</ref> first, and can only do so for time slightly later in development.

text.text: Another possibility, however, is that children apply "more" to all dimensions simultaneously when they first use the word, and that differences in performance are due to differences in task demands.

In particular, while sets of objects were presented statically and were available when the test question was posed in the Numerical Quantification Task, the actions in the Temporal Quantification Task unfolded dynamically and sequentially, requiring children to track and retain information in mind before making the quantity judgment.

Supporting the possibility that task demands may have masked comprehension of "more", a follow-up study (reported in Supplementary Study 1) found that participants performed worse on numerical quantification than temporal quantification when the objects in each set were presented sequentially over a fixed period of time, possibly due to the even greater difficulty of tracking the number of objects presented in each set over time than tracking who performs an action longer.

Although children performed above chance on the Temporal Quantification Task at 3 years of age, consistent with a linguistic comparison of temporal duration, it is also possible that children simply selected the person who finished the action last (since the actor who performed the action longer always performed it last).

Providing evidence against this possibility, a second follow-up study (reported in Supplementary Study 2) found that children selected the person who performed the action last (and longer) less often when "more" was replaced by a nonce word ("tiv") in the test question (e.g., "Who did tiv waving?"), suggesting that children's success on the Temporal Quantification Task cannot be fully explained by such a bias.

Nonetheless, in Study 2 we designed a revised version of the Temporal Quantification Task that tested children's temporal quantification when a strategy to select the person who completed the action last was not possible.
In Study 2, children completed a Temporal Quantification Task in which one person began performing an action before the other person joined in, and both ended their actions at the same time.
Here, and in Study 3, we focused on assessing the nature of children's temporal quantification.

Although one of our goals was to compare temporal quantification to other domains like number, Study 1 and Supplementary Study 1 convinced us that a perfectly controlled comparison of time vs. number might not be possible.

When sets of objects are presented statically in a numerical quantification task, children are not required to track information over time in order to make a magnitude judgment, as they are in a temporal quantification task, introducing a potential difference in task demands as a confound in the manipulation of dimension of magnitude.
This confound was present in Study 1, in which children performed better on a static numerical task than a dynamic temporal task.
But while sets of objects can be presented sequentially over time instead, a numerical quantification task employing this mode of presentation still differs in a critical way from a temporal task.
In such a version of the numerical task, objects are presented one by one, requiring children to individuate each object and update a count of objects in working memory for each actor.
In contrast, while information unfolds over time as well in the temporal task, duration is experienced continuously rather than accumulated item by item, which may be more challenging.
Children's worse performance in such a modified numerical quantification task in Supplementary Study 1 demonstrates this problem.

Given this limitation, in the remainder of this paper we aimed to create a strong test of children's ability to linguistically compare temporal magnitudes, and tested whether this ability emerged on roughly the same timeline as comparison in other domains, as reported in past work (Barner & Snedeker, 2006; Gathercole, 1985; Odic et al., 2013).

We explored this possibility in Study 3 by presenting children with scenes in which the actors alternated in performing actions that summed to an overall shorter or longer duration.

In Study 3, participants completed a revised Temporal Quantification Task in which the actors alternated performing the actions, but the sum of the durations of one actor's actions was three times greater than that of the other.

In Study 3, we found that as in Study 2, 4-year-olds but not 3-year-olds succeeded on the Temporal Quantification Task when the person who performed the action longer did not complete it last.
These results are compatible with the hypothesis that children acquire the ability to compare temporal durations with "more" at 4 years old.
Importantly, 3-year-olds did not perform below chance, as would be predicted if they deployed a strategy to select the person who performed the action last.
Three-year-olds' success in the Temporal Quantification Task in Study 1 is thus unlikely to be the result of such a bias.
Across three studies, we investigated children's ability to make "more" judgments for temporal durations, and found that this ability emerges sometime between 3 and 4 years of age.
In Study 1, children as young as 3 correctly identified an actor who performed an action "more" than a second actor.
However, in Studies 2 and 3, only 4-year-olds made accurate "more" judgments when the actor who performed the action longer did not perform it last.

These findings suggest that children are able to linguistically compare temporal durations earlier than they encode words like "second" and "hour", but around the same age (or slightly older) that they successfully compare durations in non-verbal tasks (Droit-Volet et al., 2001; Droit-Volet & Wearden, 2001) and make comparative judgments with "more" for number and continuous amount (Barner & Snedeker, 2006; Gathercole, 1985; Odic et al., 2013).

text.text: These data suggest that, by at least age 4, children are able to identify temporal durations as the relevant dimension of comparison.
This is not necessarily trivial, since most events are multi-dimensional and can be measured in multiple ways.
For example, as people walk, they produce a number of steps covering a particular distance, and do so for a particular amount of time.

Previous studies find that adults are sensitive to this ambiguity, and are able to identify multiple dimensions like number, distance, intensity, and time when asked how they would measure events like walking, dancing, and running (see Barner et al., 2008).

text.text: One question raised by this work is which abilities are involved when children compare temporal durations in natural language.
On standard semantic analyses of comparative expressions containing "more", this process involves multiple steps.

For example, to evaluate an expression like, "Kat did more waving than Hannah," listeners must represent the duration of each waving event, and then project these magnitudes onto a common scale of degrees.
These degree values are then compared, supporting the interpretation of "more" (Cresswell, 1976; Kennedy, 2007; Kennedy & McNally, 2005).

text.text: On some accounts, this scale of degrees is abstract, such that the same scale is deployed across different dimensions of measurement, permitting cross-dimensional comparison (e.g., "He is richer than he is smart"; see Bale, 2008).

text.text: Thus, in order to interpret comparative statements for events quantified by time, children must encode each duration, represent each in an analog format on the same scale, and compare these degrees.

As noted in the Introduction, the present study is relevant to understanding children's acquisition of other duration expressions, like "second", "minute", and "hour", which are acquired gradually between the ages of 4 and 7 years of age (Shatz et al., 2010; Tillman & Barner, 2015).

text.text: The present study suggests that the challenge of learning these expressions cannot be explained by factors like the salience of time, or by an inability to encode specific temporal durations.

Instead, some accounts propose that duration words like "minute" may be hard because they represent culturally mediated arbitrary divisions of time that children do not spontaneously consider as possible meanings for words (Tillman et al., 2024).

text.text: Also, previous studies suggest that such words may depend on prior mastery of exact numerical language.

Consistent with this, Tillman and Barner (2015) found that children do not represent the absolute durations of words like "minute", "hour", "day", etc., until they can explicitly state their definitions, e.g., how many minutes are in an hour.

text.text: While the main focus of this study was on children's comparison of temporal durations, it remains unclear whether the linguistic comparison of durations emerges in synchrony with comparison of other dimensions, like number and space, which emerge around 3½ years of age (Barner & Snedeker, 2006; Gathercole, 1985; Odic et al., 2013).

text.text: In Study 1, we found that 3year-olds could identify the person who kept performing an action longer as having done "more" of it.
However, when the person who did the action longer did not perform it last in Studies 2 and 3, 3-year-old children performed at chance, unlike 4-year-olds.
A conservative interpretation of these mixed findings is that 3-year-olds cannot linguistically compare temporal durations (consistent with data from Studies 2-3).
Thus, their success in Study 1 (replicated in Supplementary Study 1) may not reflect competence, but may instead reflect a bias to select the person who performed the action last.

On this view, children initially use "more" to quantify concrete domains, and only later extend its application to more abstract dimensions like time, by virtue of both the non-linguistic similarities between representations of number, space, and time, as well as grammatical similarities in how words for these different domains are used (de Hevia et al., 2014; Gentner, 2001; Lakoff & Johnson, 1980; Murphy, 1996; Smith & Sera, 1992; Spence, 2011).

text.text: It is also possible that children learn to linguistically compare magnitudes with "more" for all dimensions simultaneously, as hypothesized by Odic et al. (2013), but that children's performance across domains is modulated by differences in task demands.

(2013)</ref>, but that children's performance across domains is modulated by differences in task demands.

text.text: On this account, the success of 3-year-olds in Study 1 might reflect genuine competence, whereas their failures in Studies 2-3 reflect task demands.
Several findings support this analysis.

First, in Supplementary Study 2, children chose the person who acted both longer and last less often when "more" was replaced with a nonce word, suggesting that children's judgments with time in Study 1 could not be explained by a baseline bias to select the person who completed the action last.
Second, in Study 3, no age group performed below chance when the last actor acted for less total time, as would be expected if children had a last actor bias.
Third, we found evidence that task demands may actually mask quantification competence in 3-year-olds.
In Supplementary Study 1, children performed worse on numerical quantification than temporal quantification when actors placed objects into boxes sequentially in the numerical task.

Given that they performed well in quantifying numerical quantities in Study 1 when arrays of objects were presented statically and were visually available at test, children's poor performance in Supplementary Study 1 cannot be attributed to a lack of ability to compare numerical quantities with "more", and is instead likely the product of task demands involved in tracking dynamically presented information over time.
The current study has several limitations which should be addressed in future work.
First, while we focused our investigation on the comparative "more", children's use of other words which quantify relative duration such as "longer" should be investigated as well.
Does use of both terms arise simultaneously, and does their application across domains follow a similar trajectory?
Also, our investigation was limited to English, which uses one word "more", to compare quantities across all domains, whereas other languages use different quantifiers for different domains.
For example, in Swedish, "fler" denotes more in number while "mer" denotes more in amount.
Whether children learn to use these words simultaneously could shed light on the process of learning to use comparatives across domains.

If these quantifiers are acquired simultaneously despite different evidence for mapping word to meaning (because they operate over different types of quantities), then there may be one common bottleneck for linguistically encoding comparisons of magnitude.

But if they are acquired at different ages, then learning to encode comparisons of magnitude may be a challenge which is solved individually in each domain, with differences in the informativity of the evidence for mapping word to meaning possibly resulting in different ages of acquisition (see Gillette et al., 1999; Gleitman et al., 2005).

text.text: Finally, we controlled other domains of magnitude in the current study, such that temporal trials differed only in duration and numerical trials differed only in number.

It would be interesting to contrast who did more in different domains (e.g., one person doing an action longer vs. the other at a greater rate) and ask children and adults to make quantity judgments to understand the relative dominance of different domains in judging magnitude, and to explore the influence of extra-perceptual factors such as verb semantics (see Barner et al., 2008).

text.text: In summary, we find that children are able to quantify temporal duration with the comparative "more" by 4 years of age, several years before they master other temporal language and about the same time or slightly later than their use of "more" in the domains of number and space.
This sheds light on the mechanisms of time word learning and the reasons for which children may be delayed in learning other classes of time words, especially exact duration words.

We also suggest several avenues for future research, including further investigation on the simultaneity of children's learning of "more" across domains and exploration of cross-linguistic differences in quantification.

text.text: Participants completed a novel Temporal Quantification Task.
Children completed six trials.
On each trial, they watched a video of two people sitting behind a table performing an action (Figure 1).

text.text: The actions of the two actors differed only in their total duration, with one person performing the action for approximately six seconds and the other for approximately two seconds (3:1 ratio).
The actors alternated in performing the actions.
First, one actor performed the action for 3 seconds, and then the other actor performed it for 1 second.
This sequence was then repeated once more.
The actions performed were otherwise identical to those in Studies 1 and 2.
In half the trials, the person on the left performed the action longer and in half the trials the person on the right performed the event longer.
The experimenter told the child, "Look, Kat is waving, and Hannah is waving too."
The experimenter pointed to each person when naming them.
At the end of each trial, the experimenter asked the child, "Who did more waving?".
Children could respond either by pointing to the character or saying the character's name.
The results of Study 3 largely replicated those of Study 2.
